records.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
records.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

records.title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses
records.abstract: and  Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited. Research Design and  We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.  The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). In the overall sample, being male, married/partnered, having a household income above $28,034, and being physically active were positively associated with IC, whereas having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC (all p  Physical activity and chronic disease burden were important correlates of IC among Hispanic older adults, with some subgroup-specific patterns observed across gender, residential community, and place of birth. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic and contextual factors when promoting healthy aging among Hispanic older adults.

records.title: Admission lactate-to-albumin ratio in critically ill older adults: superior to its individual components but not additive to APACHE II — a retrospective cohort study
records.abstract: Older adults constitute a growing and heterogeneous proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, and early risk stratification in this group remains difficult. The lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) is a composite biomarker that combines a marker of acute metabolic derangement with one of physiological reserve, and has shown prognostic value in several critical care settings. Its performance in geriatric ICU patients, and specifically whether it adds information to established severity scores, has not been established.  We conducted a retrospective, single-centre cohort study of consecutive patients aged ≥ 65 years admitted to the mixed medical–surgical ICU of a tertiary referral hospital in Türkiye between January 2024 and July 2025. LAR was calculated as serum lactate (mmol/L) divided by serum albumin (g/dL), from samples obtained within the first 6 h of ICU admission. The primary outcome was all-cause 28-day mortality. Discrimination was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and curves were compared using the DeLong test. Multivariable logistic regression assessed whether LAR was independently associated with mortality after adjustment for age, sex, Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), SOFA, APACHE II and C-reactive protein (CRP).  Of 296 screened admissions, 294 were analysed; 98 patients (33.3%) died within 28 days. Non-survivors had higher admission LAR than survivors [1.37 (IQR 0.84–2.50) vs. 0.62 (IQR 0.46–0.99), p p = 0.0005) and serum albumin alone (AUC 0.656; ΔAUC 0.137, 95% CI 0.061–0.213, p = 0.0004). APACHE II discriminated considerably better than LAR (AUC 0.924, 95% CI 0.893–0.955; ΔAUC 0.131, 95% CI 0.080–0.181, p p = 0.055; likelihood ratio test p = 0.098). On univariable analysis LAR was strongly associated with mortality (OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.63–2.88, p p = 0.052). APACHE II (adjusted OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.21–1.52, p p = 0.015) remained independently associated with mortality.  In critically ill older adults, admission LAR discriminates 28-day mortality better than either of its components alone and is strongly associated with mortality on unadjusted analysis. However, it did not add significant discriminatory information to the APACHE II score, and it was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment for illness severity. LAR may be useful as a rapidly available early indicator where a full severity score is not yet computable, but on these data it does not complement APACHE II.

records.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
records.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

records.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these  underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.

records.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

records.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
records.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

records.title: Nurse-administered symptom-burden screening and 12-month mortality in older adults with heart failure: a cohort study
records.abstract: Older adults with heart failure face significant symptoms and psychosocial burdens that routine cardiology care might overlook. We assessed whether Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) and Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale (IPOS) scores can predict 12-month mortality and improve risk discrimination beyond clinical covariates in a hospital cohort from a low-resource setting.  We conducted an observational cohort study at the National Geriatric Hospital (Vietnam). Inpatients aged 60 years or older with chronic heart failure who met the eligibility criteria were approached in the order of admission (January 2021-December 2022), and ESAS (9 items, each scored 0–10) and IPOS (17 items) were completed within 48 h of admission by trained ward nurse-researchers. Vital status at 12 months was determined through medical records and structured follow-up calls. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated associations with mortality, adjusting for age, sex, heart-failure classification, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, comorbidities, and financial strain. Primary analyses used predefined categorical cutoffs (ESAS > 30; IPOS ≥ 20). Discrimination was further assessed with Harrell’s C-index and the 12-month area under the curve (AUC), and model fit was compared using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Calibration was also examined using a logistic analogue (Hosmer–Lemeshow).  Of 327 screened patients, 304 were enrolled (mean age 71.9 ± 8.8 years; 52% men); 65 deaths (21.4%) occurred within 12 months. ESAS and IPOS were strongly correlated, but there was no multicollinearity. High symptom burden (ESAS > 30) independently predicted mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 2.27; 95%CI 1.20–4.28), while high palliative-care needs (IPOS ≥ 20) were not associated (aHR: 1.04; 95%CI 0.47–2.30). Kaplan–Meier curves across ESAS–IPOS strata diverged. Including categorical patient-reported measures in the clinical model modestly improved discrimination and fit: Harrell’s C increased from 0.671 to 0.697 and 12-month AUC from 0.700 to 0.718 ( p = 0.034), with acceptable calibration and lower information criteria.  In hospitalized older adults with heart failure, a nurse-administered ESAS identified patients at independently higher 12-month mortality risk. IPOS, though clinically informative for care planning, added little prognostic information once symptom severity was considered. Brief, nurse-led symptom screening offers a feasible approach to risk stratification in resource-limited settings. Trial registration Not applicable.

records.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

records.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
records.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

records.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

records.title: Societal actors’ perceptions of intersectoral collaboration and the participation of older adults in the development of age-friendly environments
records.abstract: Older adults’ participation and intersectoral collaboration are central to the development of age-friendly environments. While previous research has emphasised the importance of these principles, less is known about how they are understood and enacted by societal actors in practice. This creates a need to explore societal actors’ perceptions of both intersectoral collaboration and older adults’ participation in the development of age-friendly environments. Method The study had a participatory qualitative design. Data were collected through a World Café involving 19 societal actors in a Swedish municipal context. Participants represented several societal sectors relevant to age-friendly environments, including welfare, care, public health, governance, social sustainability, urban planning,mobility, civil society, and voluntary engagement. Findings The findings showed that participants perceived intersectoral collaboration as requiring shared societal responsibility across multiple sectors, while responsibility risked becoming unclear when no actor had an explicit mandate to coordinate, prioritise and act. Intersectoral collaboration was viewed as a way of sharing resources, yet also as vulnerable when it relied mainly on personal relationships and informal networks rather than organisationally embedded structures. Similarly, older adults’ participation was highly valued when developing age-friendly initiatives, but participants questioned whether existing participation channels adequately reflect the diversity of older adults’ experiences and needs.  Age-friendly work requires shared responsibility across societal actors, supported by clear coordination. Personal relationships and informal networks should be recognised as valuable for enabling collaboration, but they need to be complemented by formal structures to ensure sustainability over time. Moreover, greater efforts to reach seldom-heard older adults are needed. Doing so may contribute to more nuanced and age-friendly initiatives that better reflect the diverse needs of the older population.

records.title: Safe homecoming intervention after hospital discharge: a retrospective cohort study of mortality and readmission among patients 75 years or older in Sweden
records.abstract: After a hospital stay, older patients are at increased risk of health complications that may lead to readmission to hospital or premature death. Globally, numerous interventions have been applied to enhance transitional care for older patients, but the evidence base remains inconclusive. One form of a transitional care intervention is the Swedish primary health care Safe homecoming intervention, a time-limited, interprofessional and tailored home health care intervention designed to prevent avoidable complications and readmissions following hospital discharge. The effects of Safe homecoming have not yet been scientifically evaluated. The present study aimed to assess the association between the interprofessional Safe h omecoming intervention and the risk of death or readmission.  We conducted a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study in Örebro County, Sweden, using administrative and medical-record data from 2013 to 2020. The source cohort comprised 38,338 patients aged 75 years or older who had been admitted to hospital for at least one day. We included 128 patients who received the interprofessional Safe homecoming intervention at a single primary health care centre between 1 November 2016 and 31 May 2019 and 512 propensity score-matched controls from across the county receiving standard care.  The mean age was 85.5 years, and 60.9% of patients in both groups were women. At 90 days, the cumulative incidence of first hospital readmission was 20.3% in the intervention group and 33.6% among controls (Gray’s test p = 0.005). In the competing-risk analysis, the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratio was 0.57 (95% CI 0.37–0.86; p = 0.008). The corresponding cause-specific Cox model yielded an HR of 0.55 (95% CI 0.36–0.84; p = 0.005). At 365 days, the Fine-Gray estimate was 0.79 (95% CI 0.59–1.05; p = 0.098). Mortality estimates favoured the intervention group numerically but were imprecise, with confidence intervals including the null at all evaluated follow-up times.  The Safe Homecoming intervention was associated with a lower risk of first hospital readmission at 90 days, whereas there was no clear evidence of an association with mortality or longer-term readmission. Given the observational design, small intervention sample, potential residual confounding and evaluation of multiple follow-up time points, these findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.
